data.title: Trump says US won't ban diesel exports
data.description:
President Trump said Friday that he will not ban exports of diesel after the Group of 7 (G7) major economies announced that they would release fuel from their stocks.

“Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution and so are we and we’re not going to be doing the export ban,” Trump told reporters as he prepared to depart the White House for Alabama.

“We were never going to do it,” he added of a diesel export ban.

Last week, Trump appeared to back the idea of banning exports of diesel as prices of the fuel reached new heights, saying “I’ve called for it within my people.”

However, in the days that followed, members of his administration including Energy Secretary Chris Wright, indicated that the administration did not plan to ban diesel exports.

Several officials said that an export ban could actually raise prices of some fuels like gasoline because refiners that make these fuels together could be incentivized to cut overall production.

Trump’s latest comments come after the G7, which includes the U.S., U.K., Canada, France, Germany, Italy, and Japan, said they would release 100 million barrels of fuel over the course of the next four months, including “a “frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.”

Diesel, which is particularly important for industries like farming and trucking, was averaging $6.37 per gallon on Friday, according to AAA,

Mallory Wilson contributed.

data.title: Thousands of legal immigrants lose Medicaid coverage as 'Big, Beautiful' cuts begin
data.description:
Thousands of refugees and other legal immigrants lost their health coverage on Oct. 1, becoming some of the first significant casualties of the Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill law. 

States and advocacy groups have been trying to warn immigrants who were previously eligible for Medicaid— such as refugees, asylees without a green card, survivors of domestic violence and victims of sex trafficking– that they no longer qualify.  

“This is a real shift that’s going to create a serious gap in access to healthcare services,” said Adriana Cadena, executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition. “The folks who have survived the most trauma, whether it’s war, natural disaster, or sexual assault, are going to be the folks who are going to be losing coverage.” 

Advocates say the eligibility restrictions on immigrants will mean people lose access to doctors, as well as medications and treatments for diabetes and other chronic diseases. 

Providers will lose long-time patients, and hospitals expect a spike in uninsured emergency room visits, driving up health system costs. Hospitals are required to provide emergency care regardless of immigration status and are reimbursed by Emergency Medicaid.  

The law doesn’t impact green card holders, as well as a few other small groups of immigrants. The law also doesn’t change existing state options to cover children and pregnant immigrants; states can still receive federal matching funding for these populations. 

More to come

The Medicaid eligibility restrictions are merely the first in a host of provisions that are projected to strip away government-sponsored health coverage. 

Starting next year, more than 1 million immigrants are projected to lose Affordable Care Act plan subsidies as well as Medicare coverage. 

The changes are part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, President Trump and congressional Republicans’ signature domestic policy legislation that he signed into law with much fanfare in 2025. The law is projected to cut Medicaid spending by $900 billion through 2034, largely by imposing new eligibility restrictions, work requirements, and cost sharing. 

In selling the bill to Congress, the administration argued that “illegal aliens” would be losing Medicaid.  

“The One, Big, Beautiful Bill is a generational chance to protect Medicaid for Americans by removing at least 1.4 million illegal immigrants from the program,” the White House said in a May 2025 statement.  

But undocumented immigrants already are ineligible for federally funded health coverage. 

The law also imposed restrictions on legal immigrants’ use of food stamps, Medicare and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. 

Major impact

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that the Medicaid changes would lead to roughly 100,000 lawfully present immigrants losing health insurance.  

Immigrant advocates said the actual number could be significantly higher because of the Trump administration’s slowing of green card applications; many legal immigrants will be kicked off Medicaid while they wait for their application decisions. 

According to U.S. Customs and Immigration Services, it will take an average of 30 months to process an application for permanent residence from a refugee who was admitted over a year ago. 

Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, said it was “shocking” to see Republicans try to demonize immigrants who had been admitted to the country for humanitarian reasons. 

“These are people who are among the most vulnerable and among the most vetted categories of immigrants,” D’Avanzo said.  

Federal officials said the law ensures U.S. government money is spent on Americans, and forces immigrants to be self-sufficient.  

“Immigrants must be able to support themselves and not depend on benefits paid for by hard-working American taxpayers. President Trump and this administration will always put American citizens first,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.  

Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank focused on lower immigration rates, said he supports the administration’s attempt to curtail immigrants’ use of welfare programs.  

But he said the savings from restricting immigrants from Medicaid are fairly modest. Much bigger savings would result from overhauling the entire immigration system  

“If we really want legal immigrants to use less welfare we would need to have a system that selects future immigrants based on skills who are unlikely to need welfare,’ Camarota said.   

Advocates said many of the people losing coverage will be forced to turn to emergency rooms for care, seeking treatment only when they get extremely ill or injured.  

D’Avanzo said it’s a false premise that cutting immigrants off from Medicaid saves money, because the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become Medicaid-eligible green card holders. 

“But in the meantime, they will put off preventative care. They will have sacrificed medication that controls chronic conditions. They will not have sought treatment for their diabetes or their heart disease,” D’Avanzo said. “And by the time they become Medicaid eligible again, they will have conditions that have not been treated because they could not afford to, and instead we’ll be seeing people in the emergency room.” 

Few options 

Some states and advocacy groups have been working to find alternatives to Medicaid coverage, but there aren’t many available.  

People could pay out-of-pocket at Federally Qualified Health Centers, which provide primary and preventive care regardless of immigration status and offer sliding-scale fees based on income. 

Immigrants can also purchase an Affordable Care Act plan, but the costs are often a barrier. Congressional Republicans allowed the law’s enhanced premium subsidies to expire last year, and the same group of immigrants who are now ineligible for Medicaid will also become ineligible for regularly subsidized ACA plans on Jan. 1.  

Shanteny Jackson, executive director of the Virginia Community Health Worker Association, said there are about 6,000 lawfully present immigrants in the Commonwealth who lost Medicaid coverage. 

Some may be eligible to enroll in a new program through the state’s ACA exchange that helps lower people’s premiums on top of any federal tax credits. 

But eligibility is limited to people with household incomes between 138 percent and 250 percent of the federal poverty level—between $22,025 and $39,900 for an individual or $45,540 and $82,500 for a family of four.   

Cadena, of Protecting Immigrant Families, said she worries about mixed-status households, and the trickle-down impact on U.S. citizen children. 

“Children are more likely to get care when their parents have care,” Cadena said. “So if parents are losing access to this care, then they would assume, or could believe, that the child is also losing access” even though the child would remain eligible as a U.S. citizen.  

“A quarter of all children in the United States live in immigrant families. So we could be talking about some very big numbers when we take all of this into account,” Cardena added.

data.title: Trump: Cornell students 'won't get a fair shake' with James leading probe
data.description:
President Trump criticized the appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor investigating the Cornell University rape case, arguing people “won’t get a fair shake” with her in the role.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed James to the case. James previously investigated and sued Trump, and the two have repeatedly battled in public.

“Letitia James is a corrupt person,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn en route to Alabama on Friday. 

“I feel bad for whoever she’s looking at because they won’t get a fair shake,” he added.

The president and New York attorney general have a long-running feud, which has included state lawsuits against the administration’s policies and her move to sue the Trump administration over fraud. 

Trump’s comments came hours after Hochul tapped James for the role. Hochul said she lacked confidence in the district attorney to handle the matter. 

“I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law. In the coming months, my office will dutifully carry out the responsibilities the governor has conferred upon us in this executive order. We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions,” James said at a Friday press conference alongside Hochul. 

The developments are the latest in the investigation into an alleged gang rape at a campus fraternity in 2025.

A woman who was a sophomore at Cornell at the time of the incident has sued the university, the fraternity, her own sorority and seven men she says were involved in assaulting her.

A local district attorney declined to bring charges after reviewing the matter. According to a report by The New York Times, some of the men named in the lawsuit acknowledged sexual contact with the woman but said it had been consensual.

data.title: Kansas Democratic Senate nominee says 'please, no' to Harris campaigning for him
data.description:
Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton said “please, no” on Thursday to the possibility of former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning with him ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. 

Appearing on Politico’s “The Conversation,” Hamilton discussed which national Democrats he would be willing to campaign with.

“It wasn’t like I was a huge champion for Kamala Harris,” he said. “People ask me, should she come here and campaign for you? Please, no. Don’t come here to campaign for me.”

“Harris can stay in California. Yeah, and I mean no disrespect for her. I just think she is not somebody who would win votes here in Kansas,” Hamilton added. 

While he has campaigned with Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Hamilton similarly declined the opportunity to campaign with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

He then recounted Schumer asking him what would be the biggest challenge in the Kansas Senate race. 

“I said, ‘You, you know, you are,’” he continued. “I am only saying in Kansas, you’re a liability. You’re not a, you’re not a help.”

Harris has campaigned with other Democratic candidates in battleground states, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

“Remember, the Senate seat is six years. So let’s think about that in the lives of all the people that the leaders here serve,” Harris said alongside El-Sayed at a discussion on Black maternal health care. 

Her involvement with Democratic campaigns in traditionally Red states has divided the party with former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) Senate campaign distancing itself from the former vice president.

“The VP did very well in some places and didn’t do great in others, and if you’re in a state where she didn’t perform well, it may not help you to have her campaign with you this fall,” Democratic strategist and former Harris aide Jamal Simmons told The Hill in August. 

President Trump won Kansas in 2024 by nearly 16 points over Harris but his approval rating in the Sunflower State has slipped to around 40 percent, according to a September Emerson College and Nexstar poll. 

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) is the favorite in Kansas, but the generally bad political atmostphere may have hoped a window for Hamilton.

The Emerson poll also found Hamilton polling slightly ahead of Marshall at 45 percent to 43 percent.

Kansas is generally a red state and, although it has sometimes elected moderate Democratic governors, it has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932.

data.title: LePage breaks with Trump on Iran, Canada tariffs, immigration in Maine House debate
data.description:
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R) split with the Trump administration on key issues — including the Iran war, tariffs and immigration — during a Thursday debate in the open U.S. House race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District. 

LePage, the GOP nominee, who is running against Matt Dunlap (D), the state auditor, previously criticized the administration’s widespread immigration crackdown efforts after he said his son’s father-in-law was being wrongfully deported. 

During the Thursday debate hosted by local outlet WMTW, LePage called for increased accountability and transparency from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) around its deportation operations. 

Additionally, the Republican nominee expressed disagreement with the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canada and leaned on his experience facilitating negotiations over the North American Free Trade Agreement under the first Trump administration. 

“We need to de-escalate the rhetoric, and we need to get the president and the prime minister of Canada back to the negotiating table,” LePage said. 

Despite disagreeing with the Trump administration in segments of the debate, LePage also touted his past experience working with the president during his time as governor. 

“I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said, adding, “My opponent will not.”

The GOP candidate urged the president to bring the ongoing Iran war to a close “as quick as possible,” but said he would oppose a war powers resolution if elected. The House has passed three Iran war powers resolutions with the support of several Republican lawmakers. 

Dunlap criticized LePage’s stance on a war powers resolution question, pointing to rising energy prices tied to the ongoing conflict. 

“Your heating oil is $7 a gallon because of the Iran war. Paul LePage can’t decide if he’s for it or against it,” Dunlap wrote in a social media post after the debate.

LePage and Dunlap will face off again in a second debate on Oct. 15. 

Republicans are hoping to flip this key swing district in November, which is currently represented by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden. Trump won the district by 9 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. 

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates this race as “Likely Republican.” However, recent polling has shown Dunlap leading the former governor among likely voters.

In a University of New Hampshire survey released at the end of September, the Democrat had a 6-point advantage over his GOP opponent.

data.title: Paramount, Warner Bros. reveal new name
data.description:
(KTLA) – Once the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) merger is finalized, the resulting media empire will fall under a new name.

On Friday morning, David Ellison took to social media to make the announcement.

“What once was the peak is now just the beginning,” he wrote on social platform X. “Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine.”

He added, “Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.”

The name Skydance was taken from Ellison’s film and television production company, Skydance Media. It’s not too surprising, seeing as when he joined his company with Paramount Global and National Amusements in 2025, the latter was renamed Paramount Skydance.

As for the WBD and Paramount merger, Ellison explained that the new name was chosen “for a few important reasons.”

“First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic,” he continued. “Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one.”

Instead, Ellison noted they decided they “wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own” while allowing the two entertainment giants to “remain in the spotlight.”

He also added that Skydance will “honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special,” which means “giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.”

The merger will not only bring together the two Hollywood conglomerates but also HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services, and the television networks CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central and Food Network.

“I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together,” he exclaimed.

It’s been a long journey to get here.

On Tuesday, a California federal judge resolved a lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general, which had opposed the $110 billion merger. Weeks earlier, Paramount reached a settlement in an antitrust lawsuit.

The tentative closing date for the merger is Oct. 6.

Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav is expected to leave his post. He’s reportedly set to receive more than $550 million in stock and cash once the deal closes, including $34.2 million in cash severance payments.

data.title: Grassley calls on Trump administration to ban kratom "NOW"
data.description:
Sen. Chuck Grassley (D-Iowa) on Friday called on the Trump administration to finalize its proposed rule limiting the sale of kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties that can be bought over the counter.

“All Kratom is deadly it should NOT be sold at gas stations/vape stores/ANYWHERE Admin needs 2 put out final 7OH rule NOW Kratom is killing our kids BEWARE of special interest snake oil,” Grassley said on the social media platform X.

Grassley was referring to the Drug Enforcement Administration’s proposed rule published in July that would temporarily schedule any kratom products as Schedule I substances if they contain more than 0.05 percent dry weight of 7-hydroxymitragynine, the opioid-like chemical found in kratom.

While currently not scheduled at the federal level, 11 states have banned it. Kratom is still legal for purchase in Iowa.

The DEA said in July that 7-OH “presents severe risks to public health, including tolerance, dependence and addiction.”

Kratom, or Mitragyna speciosa, originates from Southeast Asia. The plant is not currently scheduled under the Controlled Substances.

The plant is anecdotally touted as being helpful for addicts weaning themselves off opioids, but addiction organizations like American Addiction Centers do not endorse it due to the risk of dependence, a lack of regulation and potential drug interactions.

Overdoses and deaths connected to kratom are rare, though the substance was thrown back in the news last month after two University of Mississippi students were found dead near packages of kratom. It is currently unclear whether kratom was linked to their deaths, though two individuals have been charged for selling kratom in connection to the deaths.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in March published a report finding that between 2015 and 2025, kratom-related exposure reports rose by 1,200 percent.

data.title: Justice Department sues Maryland over federal agent mask ban
data.description:
The Justice Department sued Maryland on Thursday over a new law barring federal law enforcement officers from wearing masks and requiring them to identify themselves while working in the Old Line State.

The complaint, filed the same day the law took effect, argues that Maryland and two of its largest counties are illegally attempting to regulate federal officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, violating the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause.

The new state law prohibits federal, state and local law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings while on duty, with exceptions for certain operations and protective equipment.

It also requires officers to display identification on the outermost layer of their clothing and, when asked, verbally identify themselves.

Officers who violate either requirement can face civil fines of up to $1,500, according to the complaint.

The Justice Department is challenging similar restrictions in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. Prince George’s County’s law carries steeper penalties, allowing officers who violate its requirements to face a misdemeanor charge, up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $5,000.

“The Federal Government, not state and local governments, gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said Thursday.

The department argued masks and limits on displaying officers’ personal identities can protect federal agents from harassment and doxing, and prevent suspects from identifying officers involved in future enforcement operations.

The complaint cites several incidents involving federal officers in Maryland, including an August case in which a Baltimore-area deportation officer and the officer’s spouse were doxed online.

The administration made clear in the complaint that it does not intend to follow the restrictions.

“Federal law enforcement agents and officers cannot and will not comply with the Challenged Laws, which are unconstitutional and recklessly disregard officer safety, public safety, and federal operational needs,” DOJ attorneys write.

data.title: NASA's dexterous humanoid robots built to assist humans on the moon
data.description:
(NewsNation) — At NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, the 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team, is working on new machines to join crews on future lunar missions.

These robots, however, are not just built for repetitive tasks. Their objective is to act as a hands-on support team for the crew while on the moon.

“It’s really about the human elements — either working in environments designed for humans or working alongside humans. That’s our niche,” said Shaun Azimi, Dexterous Robotics Team lead. “We’re uniquely positioned to bring in folks who are designing the human environments.”

The team’s past work includes humanoids such as Robonaut 2, which spent seven years working on the International Space Station, and Valkyrie, NASA’s first bipedal humanoid. These projects gave the team experience with electronics, mechanics, mobility and dexterity.

Applications for the new humanoids also extend to future missions to Mars. Ahead of a crewed mission to the Red Planet, the Dexterous Robotics Team is set to work with other agencies in giving the public a voice on technology ideas for crewed exploration.

The humanoids will work alongside the human crew as assistants on missions to “enhance a crew’s performance and productivity while reducing risk and expanding the capabilities for space exploration” NASA said, with “a focus on robots that can complete tasks humans do with their hands.” 

“Our team is not trying to replace human explorers with robots but instead make human exploration safer and more sustainable by developing highly capable, reliable, and trustworthy robots to work in extreme environments,” Azimi continued.

He added, “If we can send more capable robots, we can reduce the risk and make people more effective in doing the things that people do best.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump brings red state blitz to Alabama; Vance plans Alaska campaign trip
data.description:
President Trump will hold a midterm rally in Mobile, Ala., Friday evening after making similar appearances in Oklahoma and Texas just the day prior.

It’s the latest stop in Trump’s multiday campaign blitz as Republicans are locked in close races ahead of November’s midterms — and both the president’s and his party’s approval ratings have slid. He is set to speak in Mobile, split between two congressional districts that Decision Desk HQ projects will lean in the GOP’s favor, at 7 p.m. EDT.

On Friday, the Republican National Committee announced Vice President Vance would head Monday to Fairbanks, Alaska, on a campaign swing. Alaska Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R) is locked in a tough reelection fight with former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and Democrat Dan J. Sullivan.

As diesel prices soar, Trump announced Friday that Europe will release diesel from its stocks.

The September jobs report out Friday morning revealed the economy added 29,000 jobs — far fewer than expected — and the unemployment rate nudged up to 4.2 percent.

Late Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor in the Cornell sexual assault case. Hochul stopped short on Friday of calling for the resignations of the president of Cornell University or the local prosecutor, though she called the school’s handling of the incident “a failure.”

Follow live below.
